Poincaré conjecture: solved by Grigori Perelman in 2002–03 (see algebraic topology). He declined the prize in 2010.

Riemann hypothesis (1859): the zeros of the zeta function, which control how evenly primes are spread, all lie on one line in the complex plane. Trillions of zeros have been checked, but no proof exists. A proof would sharpen countless results about primes.

P vs NP (1971): can every quickly checkable problem be quickly solved? (See computability.) Yang–Mills existence and mass gap: give a rigorous mathematical construction of the quantum theory behind the strong nuclear force and prove its lightest particle has positive mass. Hodge conjecture: certain topological features of algebraic shapes come from algebraic sub-shapes. Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer: the number of rational points on an elliptic curve is predicted by its L-function.

Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (developing, November 2026): must smooth fluid flows in 3D stay smooth, or can they “blow up”? In September 2026 OpenAI announced an AI-generated, Lean-checked proof that the equations can blow up when a carefully designed smooth external force is applied, a case the Clay statement allows but many experts consider an artificial loophole. NYU’s Tristan Buckmaster, whose related work came first, disputes how OpenAI reached its method. On 20 November 2026 Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge posted a claimed AI-assisted proof of blow-up with no force at all, with some verification materials still to come. Neither claim has been independently verified, and Clay has not awarded a prize. Disclosure: this Lab’s text is drafted with Claude, made by Anthropic, where Alpöge works; the authors report using Claude.
1796–1801 — Carl Friedrich Gauss: Proved quadratic reciprocity, which he called the “golden theorem”.
1940 and 1967 — André Weil; Robert Langlands: Weil’s letter on mathematical analogies; Langlands’ letter launching the program. Langlands received the Abel Prize in 2018.
1990–2010 — Vladimir Drinfeld; Laurent Lafforgue; Ngô Bảo Châu: Fields Medals for function-field cases and the “fundamental lemma” (2008).
1995 and 2018 — Andrew Wiles; Peter Scholze: Modularity for Fermat; new p-adic geometry (Fields Medal 2018) and, with Laurent Fargues, a geometric approach to local Langlands.
2024 — Gaitsgory, Raskin and seven co-authors: Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture.

In 1967 Robert Langlands, then a young professor at Princeton, wrote a 17-page letter to André Weil proposing deep connections between two worlds. On one side: Galois groups, the symmetries of solutions to polynomial equations, which govern counting solutions modulo primes. On the other: automorphic forms, highly symmetric functions studied with harmonic analysis.

The simplest case is centuries old. Quadratic reciprocity (Gauss, 1796) links whether p is a square modulo q to whether q is a square modulo p. Langlands’ conjectures extend this kind of hidden harmony to all equations and all symmetry groups.

Modularity, used to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem, is one case: the number of solutions of an elliptic curve modulo each prime matches the coefficients of a modular form. You can check one example yourself: the curve y² + y = x³ − x² and the form q ∏(1 − qⁿ)²(1 − q¹¹ⁿ)² agree prime by prime.

There are parallel versions for number fields, for function fields and for geometry (the “Rosetta stone” Weil described in 1940). In 2024 a team of nine mathematicians led by Dennis Gaitsgory and Sam Raskin proved the geometric Langlands conjecture in five papers totalling over 800 pages, after about 30 years of work. The number-theory version remains largely open.

topic: The abc conjecture and a disputed proof
claim: The abc conjecture (Masser and Oesterlé, 1985–88) is about equations a + b = c in whole numbers with no common factor. Multiply the distinct primes dividing a, b and c to get rad(abc). Usually c is smaller than rad(abc). The conjecture says c can exceed rad(abc)^(1 + ε) only finitely often, for any ε > 0. Example: 1 + 8 = 9 has rad(1·8·9) = 6 < 9, a rare “hit”. If true, abc would imply many other results at once, including a version of Fermat’s Last Theorem for large exponents.

topic: The abc conjecture and a disputed proof
claim: In 2012 Mochizuki, at Kyoto University’s RIMS, posted four papers (over 500 pages) developing inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUT) and claiming a proof. Few could follow them. In 2018 Peter Scholze and Jakob Stix visited Kyoto and reported a serious gap in Corollary 3.12, the key step. Mochizuki replied that they had misunderstood. The papers were published in 2021 in PRIMS, a journal based at his own institute where he is chief editor; the editors said he was not involved in handling them.

topic: The abc conjecture and a disputed proof
claim: Since then, Kirti Joshi has argued that Scholze and Stix’s objections are wrong but that Mochizuki’s proof is incomplete, and has proposed his own completion; Mochizuki rejects Joshi’s account. In 2026 a project at Japan’s ZEN University (Project LANA) began working toward computer verification of IUT and issued an interim report that declined to rush to a verdict (developing).

topic: The abc conjecture and a disputed proof
claim: The outcome so far: outside Kyoto, most number theorists do not regard abc as proved. The case shows how mathematics settles disputes: not by authority or publication alone, but by whether experts can follow and check every step, and increasingly by computer verification.

topic: Famous open problems and recent breakthroughs
claim: Still open: the twin prime conjecture (infinitely many primes two apart, like 11 and 13); the Goldbach conjecture (every even number above 2 is a sum of two primes, checked up to 4 × 10¹⁸); the Collatz conjecture (halve if even, triple and add one if odd: do you always reach 1?); whether π + e is irrational.

topic: Famous open problems and recent breakthroughs
claim: Recent progress on old problems: In 2013 Yitang Zhang, then a little-known lecturer, proved there are infinitely many prime pairs less than 70 million apart; collaborative work (Polymath) and James Maynard cut the gap to 246. Also in 2013 Harald Helfgott proved the “weak” Goldbach conjecture for odd numbers. In 2019 Terence Tao proved that almost all Collatz sequences get close to small values.

topic: Famous open problems and recent breakthroughs
claim: Settled: Maryna Viazovska solved sphere packing in 8 dimensions in 2016 (and, with colleagues, in 24), earning a Fields Medal in 2022. In February 2025 Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture about how small a region can be while containing a needle pointing in every direction; Wang received a 2026 Fields Medal. Yu Deng, with Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma, rigorously derived the Boltzmann equation for gases from particle dynamics, progress on Hilbert’s sixth problem; Deng also received a 2026 Fields Medal.

topic: Famous open problems and recent breakthroughs
claim: Amateurs still contribute. In 2023 David Smith, a retired print technician and hobbyist, found the first single tile that covers the plane only without repeating (the “hat”), proved with three professional collaborators. In 2024 an online collaboration, largely of amateurs, determined the fifth busy beaver number.

topic: AI and the future of proof (developing)
claim: In 2024 DeepMind’s AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry reached silver-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad; in 2025 systems from Google DeepMind and OpenAI reached gold-medal level. By 2026 AI tools were helping move Erdős problems (hundreds of open questions posed by Paul Erdős) to “solved”. Terence Tao noted that much of the early help was smart literature search, finding old papers that already contained answers, but AI also produced new proofs, and in May 2026 a Google DeepMind agent reported solving 9 of 353 Erdős problems it attempted, with Lean-checked proofs.

topic: AI and the future of proof (developing)
claim: In September 2026 OpenAI announced a claimed Navier–Stokes blow-up proof produced by many AI agents and checked in Lean (see the Millennium page). Mathematicians praised parts of the result but raised concerns: whether the forced case meets the spirit of the problem, whether Lean statements match the ordinary-language problem, the cost of the computation, and credit for human researchers whose methods it followed.

topic: AI and the future of proof (developing)
claim: Formal verification is central to trusting AI mathematics: a computer can check every step of a Lean proof. But the check covers only what was formally stated, and translating informal statements correctly is hard. In June 2026 a group of mathematicians issued the Leiden Declaration on AI and mathematics, setting out principles for responsible use.

topic: AI and the future of proof (developing)
claim: What does this mean for learners? Calculation and routine proof are increasingly automated, so the human advantages shift toward choosing good questions, judging whether a statement is the right one, understanding why results are true, and explaining them. Those are exactly the skills this path tries to build. Using AI for hints and checking, not for answers you have not understood, keeps you learning.

topic: How research mathematics works (and how to take part)
claim: Discovery usually starts with examples and data. As a teenager Gauss studied tables of primes and guessed that primes near N occur with density about 1/ln N; it took a century to prove (the prime number theorem, 1896). Conjectures come from patterns; proofs explain them.

topic: How research mathematics works (and how to take part)
claim: Research is mostly failure. A mathematician may spend years on a problem, trying approaches that collapse. Andrew Wiles worked on Fermat in secret for seven years, announced a proof, found a gap, and needed another year with Richard Taylor to repair it.

topic: How research mathematics works (and how to take part)
claim: Results are shared as preprints on arXiv (since 1991), then refereed by journals, which can take years. Errors are found after publication too. Collaboration has grown: online Polymath projects (from 2009) involve dozens of people, and proof assistants let hundreds contribute to one formal proof.

topic: How research mathematics works (and how to take part)
claim: Who gets to do mathematics has changed and is still uneven. Sophie Germain wrote under a male name; Srinivasa Ramanujan, a clerk in Madras, reached Cambridge through a letter to G. H. Hardy in 1913; the first woman to win a Fields Medal was Maryam Mirzakhani in 2014. You can join in now: explore patterns in the OEIS, try Project Euler and Erdős problems, formalize mathematics in Lean, or make a conjecture from data in the Lab and test it.
1940s — British and American wartime teams: Operations research for convoys, radar and bombing; George Dantzig created the simplex method in 1947 for US Air Force planning.

topic: Parts of a whole: fractions, decimals, percents and ratios
claim: Decimals are fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000 and so on: 0.37 = 37/100. Percent means “per hundred”, so 37% = 37/100 = 0.37. A ratio compares two amounts: a recipe with 2 cups of flour to 1 cup of sugar has a 2:1 ratio. Ratios are fractions in disguise: sugar is ⅓ of the mix.
Robotics and vision: Solving polynomial systems for arm positions and camera geometry

Cryptography: Security proofs show a code is as hard to break as a known hard problem
Computing: Binary place value (base 2) is how every computer stores numbers

No real number squares to −1, so mathematicians defined one: i, with i² = −1. A complex number has a real part and an imaginary part: 3 + 2i. Add them like ordinary expressions: (3 + 2i) + (1 − 5i) = 4 − 3i. Multiply them using i² = −1: (3 + 2i)(1 − i) = 3 − 3i + 2i − 2i² = 5 − i.

topic: Axiomatic set theory and the sizes of infinity
claim: Paradoxes such as Russell’s forced mathematicians to choose careful axioms. The standard system, ZFC (Zermelo–Fraenkel with the axiom of choice), underlies almost all mathematics. Gödel (1940) showed the continuum hypothesis cannot be disproved from ZFC, and Paul Cohen (1963) showed it cannot be proved either. It is independent: ZFC simply does not decide it.
Mathematics: Each problem organizes decades of research

Why can’t you continuously shrink the doughnut’s hole away? A loop around the hole cannot slide off without cutting the surface. Its class in the fundamental group is not the identity, which is a topological invariant.
2009 — Jacob Lurie: Higher Topos Theory, a foundational text for ∞-categories.

Shapes defined by polynomials have rigid structure: they can be studied through the rings of polynomial functions on them (tier 6’s Nullstellensatz). Algebra makes the theory work over any number system, which is exactly what number theory needs, and geometry supplies intuition about dimension, curves and intersections.

topic: Discrete mathematics: logic, sets, counting and graphs
claim: How many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 10 people? Order doesn’t matter: C(10, 3). = 10 × 9 × 8 / (3 × 2 × 1) = 120.

Conics turn up everywhere. Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. A parabolic dish sends every incoming ray to one point, which is how satellite dishes and solar cookers work. A ball thrown in the air follows a parabola.

An infinite series converges if its partial sums settle on a number. ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … converges to 1. The harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + … does not: it grows forever, though incredibly slowly. Tests such as the ratio test tell you which is which.

claim: c. 250 BCE and 5th century — Archimedes; Zu Chongzhi: Archimedes trapped π between 223/71 and 22/7 using 96-sided polygons; in China, Zu Chongzhi found 355/113, correct to six decimals.

Some problems are combinatorial: the best order to visit 50 cities (the travelling salesperson problem) has more possible tours than there are atoms on Earth. No known method solves all such problems quickly; operations researchers use clever bounds and heuristics, and it connects to the P vs NP question.

Take f(x) = x². Over a small step h, the change is (x + h)² − x² = 2xh + h². Divide by h: 2x + h. As h → 0 this approaches 2x. So the derivative of x² is 2x: at x = 3 the curve is climbing at slope 6.

topic: Parts of a whole: fractions, decimals, percents and ratios
claim: Multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number does not change its value (2/4 = 1/2) because you are cutting every piece into the same number of smaller pieces. That is why common denominators work. Dividing by a fraction equals multiplying by its flip because division asks “how many of these fit?”: how many quarters fit in one whole? Four. So ÷ ¼ is the same as × 4.

A ramp rises at 6° and is 10 m long. How high does it climb? Opposite = hypotenuse × sin θ. 10 × sin 6° ≈ 10 × 0.1045 ≈ 1.05 m.

A Taylor polynomial is built so its value, slope, curvature and higher derivatives all match the function at one point. Matching more derivatives makes it hug the curve over a wider range. Taylor’s theorem bounds the error, so you know how many terms you need.

A car uses 6 litres per 100 km. How much for 350 km? Unit rate: 6/100 = 0.06 litres per km. 0.06 × 350 = 21 litres.
